newsitem.title: USA: Humans inhabited Siberia earlier than thought.
newsitem.headline: Humans inhabited Siberia earlier than thought.

text.p: As far back as 300,000 years ago, human beings had developed the survival skills necessary to inhabit an environment as hostile as northern Siberia, anthropologists said on Thursday.
Humans inhabited Siberia 250,000 to 300,000 years ago -- much earlier than the generally accepted date of 30,000 years ago, according to research appearing in Friday's edition of the journal Science.

"What this indicates is that people had the ability to deal with a rigorous environment like Siberia. They could control fire, have a survival strategy, make and find shelter, clothing, boots, etc.," said Michael Waters of Texas A & M University, who helped date the Diring Yuriakh site along Siberia's Lena River.

"There was a full range of behaviours that we didn't give credit for until the upper Paleolithic age, 30,000 years ago," added Waters, a geo-anthropologist. He said Diring is the oldest dated site in Siberia.
Asked why primitive people would live there, he said, "That's what I'd like to know too."
The findings raise fascinating -- and not immediately answerable -- questions about how early people got there, and what happened to them over the next quarter-million years.
Waters said it takes years to excavate such a site, because it is in permafrost. The team has to uncover one layer, and wait for it to defrost before they can proceed.
"It takes a lot of patience, and a terrific amount of sheer will to do this kind of research," he said.

Waters suspects that the first inhabitants came there in an interglacial period. Whether humans inhabited the region continuously or were pushed out by another glacial period is at this point an unknown.
Diring is the same latitude as Fairbanks, Alaska. Temperatures drop to minus 70 Fahrenheit (minus 56 C) in the winter.

Waters used a technique called thermoluminescence to date the sand around stone artifacts at the site, which was a quarry. The early inhabitants gathered chunks of quartzite there, and chipped them into crude tools.

The site was discovered in 1981 by Russian archaeologist Yuri Mochanov of the Yakutish Academy of Sciences. There has been a lot of uncertainty about how old it was, with 30,000 years being the most accepted estimate, according to Waters.
Waters' research was done with colleagues at the University of Illinois. Their work was funded in part by National Geographic Society.
